say.en: A pure silicon crystal barely conducts when cold. Warm it a little and its current rises sharply. Where do the extra carriers come from? In this lesson: Describe covalent bonding in Si and Ge.
Explain the generation of electron-hole pairs.
Relate n i and conductivity to temperature.

body.en: Silicon and germanium are tetravalent. In the crystal each atom shares its four valence electrons with four neighbours in *covalent bonds*. Thermal energy breaks a few bonds: each break frees one electron and leaves one hole, a vacancy that behaves like a positive charge. So in a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor $n = p = n_i$.

points.en: One broken bond = one free *electron* + one hole

narration.en: Each silicon atom forms four covalent bonds. Heat breaks a few of them, and each break makes one free electron and one hole, so n equals p equals n i.
narration.kn: ಪ್ರತಿ ಸಿಲಿಕಾನ್ ಪರಮಾಣು ನಾಲ್ಕು ಸಹವೇಲೆನ್ಸೀಯ ಬಂಧಗಳನ್ನು ರಚಿಸುತ್ತದೆ. ಉಷ್ಣದಿಂದ ಕೆಲವು ಬಂಧಗಳು ಮುರಿದು ಪ್ರತಿಯೊಂದರಿಂದ ಒಂದು ಮುಕ್ತ ಎಲೆಕ್ಟ್ರಾನ್ ಮತ್ತು ಒಂದು ರಂಧ್ರ ಉಂಟಾಗುತ್ತವೆ; ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ n = p = nᵢ.

title.en: Bonds, electrons and holes in pure silicon

say.en: Each silicon atom shares its four valence electrons with four neighbours. The double lines are covalent bonds, each holding two electrons.
Heat breaks one bond. The electron becomes free, and the empty place it leaves is a hole that acts like a positive charge.
In a pure crystal electrons and holes are always made in pairs, so n equals p equals n i.
Both carriers carry current. Higher temperature breaks more bonds, so n i rises and the resistance falls.

title.en: Intrinsic silicon: pairs made by heat

narration.en: Heat breaks a few covalent bonds; each break makes a free electron (yellow) and a hole (white), so n = p = ni. ni = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³ at 300 K and rises steeply with temperature, so the resistance falls. Apply a field: electrons drift one way, holes the other. Dot numbers grow with log ni.

body.en: Under a field, free electrons move in the *conduction* band and holes move in the valence band as neighbouring electrons hop into them. Both add to the current: $\sigma = e\,n_i(\mu_n + \mu_p)$. As temperature rises, nᵢ rises steeply, so the resistance of a semiconductor falls: it has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance. Electrons and holes also recombine, so at each temperature nᵢ settles at a steady value.

points.en: Higher T → more pairs → lower resistance

narration.en: Both electrons and holes carry current. A rise in temperature makes many more pairs, so a semiconductor's resistance falls as it gets hotter.
narration.kn: ಎಲೆಕ್ಟ್ರಾನ್‌ಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ರಂಧ್ರಗಳು ಎರಡೂ ಪ್ರವಾಹವನ್ನು ಸಾಗಿಸುತ್ತವೆ. ತಾಪ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿದಂತೆ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಜೋಡಿಗಳು ಉಂಟಾಗಿ ಅರೆವಾಹಕದ ರೋಧ ಕಡಿಮೆಯಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

say.en: Let us solve this together. Pure silicon at 300 kelvin has n i equals 1.5 times 10 to the power 10 centimetres to the power minus 3, micro n equals 1350 square centimetres per volt s and micro p equals 480 square centimetres per volt s. Find its conductivity and resistivity. (e equals 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 C).
sigma equals e n i micro n plus micro p equals 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 times 1.5 times 10 to the power 10 times 1350 plus 480.
sigma equals 2.4 times 10 to the power minus 9 times 1830 is approximately 4.39 times 10 to the power minus 6 S over cm.
rho equals 1/ sigma is approximately 2.28 times 10 to the power 5 ohms cm.
So the answer is sigma is approximately 4.4 times 10 to the power minus 6 S over cm; rho is approximately 2.3 times 10 to the power 5 ohms cm.
